transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-06-11 14:00 PDT
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Cerulean CTO), Priya Mehta (Cerulean Platform Eng), Diego Ramos (Cerulean SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to correlate tail (p95/p99) spikes seen in Cerulean's internal app when traffic crosses multiple network segments; focus areas: streaming vs non-streaming, batching behavior, KV cache locality/hot-shard, quantization throughput tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem networking effects.

Topics covered:
- Observed p95/p99 numbers and variance by path
- How streaming output chunking interacts with batching and prefix cache lookups
- Network hop amplification and TLS/handshake overheads inside VPC mesh
- Quantization impacts on CPU/GPU scheduling and tail jitter
- Actionable tests to reproduce and narrow root cause

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, we scheduled 68 minutes so we can get into the traces and then action items. Ethan's gonna drive the deep dive.
[00:10] Ethan: yeah hi all, quick agenda — walk through the p95/p99 snapshots you sent, run through the multi-segment path hypothesis, then propose a controlled test matrix. sound ok?
[00:18] Liam: yep sounds good. we've been seeing users hit intermittent 300-700ms p99 spikes for short queries, p95 is usually around 120ms. curious if this is mostly network or runtime.
[00:28] Priya: to add, the baseline single-region tests (no VPC peering) sit at p95~90ms p99~200ms which is fine. the big jumps happen once requests traverse our inter-region mesh and hit an on-prem transformer host for some pre/post-processing.
[00:40] Ethan: ok that aligns with multi-hop amplification. quick note — in our internal tests we see that each additional network hop adds a variable 15-45ms median, but the multiplicative effect on p99 is worse when combined with small batch sizes and streaming flushes.
[00:55] Diego: when you say streaming flushes do you mean the chunk size? we do streaming with 64-token chunk flushes currently.
[01:03] Ethan: right, streaming chunk and early-flush behavior. if the serving runtime is configured to flush on token boundaries and the request gets queued waiting for batch, you get cross-interaction where the KV cache lookup happens during batch assembly and one slow KV lookup can hold up an entire batch causing head-of-line blocking — that's a common tail source.
[01:25] Priya: we have a Redis-based KV cache inside the VPC, some prefix caches on-host, but the hot keys sometimes get routed to a different availability zone due to our load-balancer topology. could that explain hot-hot shard effects?
[01:36] Ethan: yes, absolutely. if the KV lookup crosses a network hop (AZ boundary) then the extra serialization and TLS handshake issues can add 40-100ms depending on connection reuse. also we saw serialization overhead when using mTLS with mutual cert renewals on short-lived connections — connection churn matters.
[01:58] Liam: interesting. what about batching? we've kept batch size tiny for latency, but maybe that's backfiring.
[02:05] Ethan: small batches minimize median but can raise p99 because the serving runtime's overhead per batch is relatively fixed — context setup, kernel selection, kv cache calls. for GPU models we recommend continuous batching with dynamic time-window batching (e.g., 5-10ms aggregation) rather than fixed tiny batches. that reduces per-request variance.
[02:25] Diego: in our on-prem portion we use int8 quantization for cost. any gotchas there?
[02:30] Ethan: quantization reduces raw compute time, but it can increase variance due to kernel selection and memory bandwidth patterns. for example, int8 paths sometimes cause micro-queueing on PCIe if you mix quantized and non-quantized variants on the same GPU NUMA boundary. result: occasional 2-3x slowdown for some inference shards which shows up at p99.
[02:52] Priya: that matches what we see when batches occasionally cross to a node with old driver versions.
[02:58] Ethan: drivers and CUDA/ROCm versions matter — we should confirm kernel footprints. one mitigation is isolating quantized workloads to dedicated pools (Redwood Dedicated style) so they don't compete.
[03:12] Liam: can you show one of the p99 traces?
[03:15] Ethan: sure — I pulled the trace from your upload. paging that now. (link shared: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/cerulean-06-11)
[03:22] Ethan: here's a representative p99 request: timestamps truncated for clarity — request enters edge LB (12ms), TLS handshake reused (8ms), request crosses VPC peering (30ms), hits mid-tier preproc host (40ms), then hits model host which does KV prefix lookup (120ms) because the cache mis-routed the key, then batch assembly waits 25ms for other tokens, runtime kernel dispatch 18ms, token generation streaming chunks cause small flushes of 6-12ms each. total ~367ms in this trace.
[03:55] Priya: that 120ms KV lookup seems huge. is that a Redis miss that falls back to our DB?
[04:01] Diego: yes some of our keys expire aggressively and fall back to a fallback store which is on a different subnet.
[04:06] Ethan: ok so two large contributors: cross-subnet KV fallback path and batch head-of-line blocking. both amplify p99.
[04:12] Maya: any quick wins we can try in parallel?
[04:15] Ethan: yes. quick wins: 1) pin KV hotspots to the same AZ as the model hosts (or use local in-memory prefix cache for top N keys), 2) enable connection pooling / persistent connections for KV (avoid mTLS short-lived churn), 3) switch to dynamic batching windowing so batch assembly waits micro-milliseconds but not long enough to cause user-facing median spikes, 4) experimentally increase streaming chunk size from 64->128 tokens to reduce flush overhead (but watch median token latency).
[04:44] Priya: what's the tradeoff for increasing chunk size? we're worried about perceived latency for early tokens.
[04:49] Ethan: larger chunk sizes reduce per-token overhead and flush frequency — lowers p99 in practice for multi-hop setups, but increases time-to-first-token slightly. if you prioritize immediate first-token you keep small chunks, but if p99 is killing user experience you shift chunking to 96-128 and tune early-flush heuristics (e.g., N tokens OR X ms).
[05:10] Liam: do you have numbers from Redwood's internal IT that show the p99 improvement?
[05:14] Ethan: yes — in an internal sim where we add an extra network hop (simulating peering) we saw p99 drop from ~520ms to ~220ms after moving hot-key cache local + enabling dynamic batching. median changed only a few ms. I'll attach the CSV.
[05:26] Maya: Ethan will share that CSV and the raw traces.
[05:30] Diego: another question — TLS and CPU overhead on the on-prem preprocessor node; could TLS CPU cost be a real contributor at p99 under burst?
[05:38] Ethan: absolutely; TLS handshakes and CPU user-space context switching can spike on small nodes. offload TLS to the edge LB where possible and ensure keep-alives to avoid repeated handshakes. Also check your MTU and path MTU discovery—fragmentation increases CPU and serialization time.
[05:58] Priya: network capture we did showed occasional 1500->1200 MTU mismatch paths across a partner link which caused fragmentation for larger payloads.
[06:06] Ethan: fragmentation can add large variable latency. target consistent MTU across the path.
[06:10] Liam: ok, so plan: we pin hot KV keys, enable connection pooling, tweak chunk size, run controlled on-prem harness. anything else?
[06:18] Ethan: one more subtle thing — when you mix streaming and non-streaming client modes, the runtime chooses slightly different kernel and memory layouts. if your client sometimes requests a streaming path, that will flip code paths and cause cold caches on the GPU for a few requests which show up at p99. prefer consistent client patterns or use explicit route separation.
[06:37] Priya: noted. we'll standardize client behavior for the pilot.
[06:40] Maya: let's capture concrete test matrix and owners. Diego you agreed to run on-prem harness?
[06:45] Diego: yep. I'll run the harness with the provided script, 30s warmup, 5k requests steady, then capture p95/p99 and tcpdump.
[06:52] Ethan: I'll provide the harness and the 'cerulean-06-11-benchmarks.csv' plus the p99 trace set.
[06:58] Liam: do we need Redwood Private to fix this? or Dedicated?
[07:03] Ethan: not necessarily — many of these fixes are topology and config changes. Redwood Private/Dedicated helps by giving you isolated pools (less noisy neighbor) and simpler network locality, but you can also achieve most wins via KV locality, connection pooling, and batching tweaks on your existing infra.
[07:20] Priya: ok makes sense. about quantization and driver mismatch — can you send a short doc with recommended driver/runtime matrix?
[07:27] Ethan: yes, we'll send a compatibility matrix and recommended kernel configs for int8/int4 artifacts.
[07:33] Maya: quick note, Priya asked about security/compliance if we suggest pooling or connection reuse — Diego any worries?
[07:40] Diego: mTLS is fine if we keep long-lived connections authenticated; we just need to ensure renewal windows are aligned and cert rotation doesn't drop connections. I'll coordinate with security.
[07:50] Maya: perfect. i'm going to do a quick recap and next steps.
[07:53] Maya: recap: 1) primary p99 contributors are cross-subnet KV fallbacks and batch head-of-line blocking; 2) quick wins: pin KV keys local, enable persistent connections, dynamic batch windows, increase streaming chunk size for a pilot; 3) parallel test: customer runs on-prem harness with network capture, Redwood shares CSV and traces, both dig into p99 root cause.
[08:16] Liam: sounds good. any blockers on our side?
[08:19] Priya: just scheduling time for SRE to run the harness this week.
[08:22] Maya: action items and owners we covered. we'll follow up in email with attachments. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
